title: Some Falls in Trinity Park Get a Home Tour. Others Get a Concert in the Park.
summary: Trinity Park's Home Tour returns only every other year. Here's how the ticketed tour funds park upkeep and what fills the off years instead.
body_markdown:
Trinity Park's biggest neighborhood event does not happen every year. The Home Tour, a tradition that dates back to a single Sunday afternoon in October 1975, runs on a two-year cycle. It was called off in 2020, came back in 2022, ran again in October 2024, and by that rhythm belongs on the calendar again this fall. The neighborhood calendar also includes Rock in the Park, a smaller, free concert that started almost by accident in a patch of grass that had just turned fifty.


Most guides to this neighborhood describe it as a collection of amenities: a park, a trail, a walk to Ninth Street. But the neighborhood’s calendar is also worth a closer look. Trinity Park's social calendar is not steady output from a city department. It is run by two volunteer groups, the Trinity Park Neighborhood Association and the Trinity Park Foundation, and includes both the biennial Home Tour and Rock in the Park.


## The Calendar Has Two Speeds


Some of what TPNA runs happens every single year without variation. The Spring Egg Hunt lands in April. National Night Out shows up in summer. Halloween brings out the decorating tradition the neighborhood is known for, with some blocks going well past a few pumpkins on the porch. Luminaria Night closes the year in December, timed to a single Sunday with a rain date built in, and residents pre-order candle bags weeks ahead through the Foundation.


Then there is the one event that does not repeat annually. The Home Tour is the only fixture on the calendar that takes a year off on purpose, and that gap is not an oversight. It is how the Foundation paces its bigger asks of the neighborhood. Ticket sales from one tour are meant to carry operations and capital projects through two full years, not one, which is part of why the tour does not need to happen every fall to stay relevant.


## What Nine Houses and Two Congregations Bought


The 2024 tour, held Sunday, October 20, opened up nine homes scattered from Albemarle Street up to North Duke Street, plus two houses of worship, Beth El Synagogue and Watts Street Baptist Church, and the park itself, which was marking its fiftieth year. About 600 people bought tickets. Another 50 neighbors worked it as volunteers, docents, and ticket sellers. The tour raised roughly $18,000.


That number is not just a fundraising total. It is a maintenance budget for public space that the city does not fully fund on its own. Past tours have paid for new plantings, benches, and safety fencing inside the park, a public art piece called the Bug Walk, a sculptural neighborhood map that now serves as the park's sign, and a new neighborhood marker in the median at Main Street and Buchanan Boulevard. The 2024 proceeds went toward restoring the granite steps at the park's entrance on West Trinity Avenue and toward keeping the Foundation running for the two years until the next tour.


The theme that year, "If This House Could Talk," had homeowners posting handwritten signs on their lawns sharing a story about the house itself, a format borrowed from a project that started in Cambridge, Massachusetts and has since spread to other cities. It turned the tour into something closer to an oral history walk than a real estate showcase, with homeowners narrating additions, renovations, and decades of tenants rather than square footage.


## A Smaller Concert on the Neighborhood Calendar


Rock in the Park is a smaller, free concert on the neighborhood calendar. The first one happened on September 29, 2024, with neighbors setting up lawn chairs to hear music played by residents of the neighborhood itself, no outside booking agent involved. Alsie's ice cream truck parked nearby for the afternoon. It read less like a produced event and more like a block party that happened to have a stage.


Here is roughly how the two events compare:


Home Tour Rock in the Park


Signature event Nine homes, two congregations, ticketed Free concert, bring a chair


Who performs or hosts Homeowners opening their doors Neighborhood musicians


What it funds Multi-year capital projects and Foundation operations Nothing beyond the afternoon itself


Scale About 600 attendees, 50 volunteers A crowd on the lawn


Neither event is a downgrade from the other. They are doing different jobs. The tour raises money for things that take years to plan and pay for. Rock in the Park exists because a park that just turned fifty needed an excuse to be used on a Sunday afternoon, and it turned out neighbors were happy to provide the music themselves.


## The Park Itself Is Part of the Story


None of this works without the park staying in decent shape, and that upkeep is also handled closer to home than most residents probably assume. In February 2026, the Foundation closed the grass area for a month to have it reseeded by a landscaping company called Pleasant Green Grass, according to Foundation president Karalyn Colopy. The gazebo got a fresh coat of paint ahead of the 2024 tour. A native plant garden went in near the West Trinity Avenue entrance. These are small line items, but they are the kind of maintenance that in most neighborhoods gets handled by tax dollars and a public works schedule. Here it runs through ticket sales and a handful of volunteers who also happen to be your neighbors.


The park sits inside a neighborhood built, unusually for this part of Durham, to hold every kind of housing at once: single family homes, duplexes, townhomes, and apartments on the same blocks. That mix is part of why the tour and the concert series both work as neighborhood-wide events rather than events for one type of household. A renter three blocks off Ninth Street and a homeowner on a Home Tour stop are drawing from the same small pool of volunteers and the same two organizations.


## What's Actually Ahead This Season


If the two-year pattern holds, this is a tour year, which means the Foundation should be finalizing routes and ticket details sometime this fall, likely announced through TPNA's own channels rather than anywhere else. Halloween decorating will happen regardless of which year it is, as will Luminaria Night in December, timed to a single Sunday with supply pre-orders closing about a week ahead.


For anyone who wants to work fall into a longer walk, the Duke East Campus Loop runs along the edge of the neighborhood for 1.6 miles, and the South Ellerbe Creek Trail sits just beyond that. Both connect naturally to a Sunday spent checking out Home Tour stops or wandering over from Rock in the Park to grab something on Ninth Street afterward.


The through-line is that Trinity Park's calendar was never meant to look the same every year. The Home Tour returns every two years, while other neighborhood events fill out the calendar. The neighborhood's park, its gazebo, its granite steps, and its newest garden bed reflect the ongoing maintenance that this volunteer-led calendar helps support.
